questions.q: What does a subnet mask actually define?
options: The physical location of the device
Which bits of an IPv4 address are the network portion vs. the host portion
The MAC address of the gateway
questions.explain: A subnet mask uses binary 1s to mark the network portion of an address and 0s to mark the host portion — that's the split that determines which addresses are on the same subnet.

questions.q: What does /24 mean in CIDR notation?
options: A subnet mask of 255.255.255.0 — 24 network bits
questions.explain: /24 means 24 bits are the network portion, equivalent to a 255.255.255.0 subnet mask, leaving 8 host bits (256 addresses, 254 usable).

questions.q: In the subnet 192.168.1.0/26, what is the broadcast address?
questions.explain: A /26 gives a block size of 64; the first subnet runs 192.168.1.0 to 192.168.1.63, so .0 is the network address and .63 (all host bits set to 1) is the broadcast address.

questions.q: Why can't the network address or broadcast address of a subnet be assigned to a host?
options: They're reserved by the router manufacturer
The network address identifies the subnet itself, and the broadcast address reaches every host on it — neither identifies one specific host
They're always used by the DNS server
It's an arbitrary rule with no technical reason
questions.explain: The network address (all host bits 0) identifies the subnet as a whole, and the broadcast address (all host bits 1) is used to reach every device on the subnet — neither can uniquely identify a single host.

questions.q: Beyond conserving addresses, why does subnetting matter for security?
options: It doesn't have any security benefit
It lets you place different device groups in separate subnets with different firewall rules and monitoring, instead of one flat network
It prevents all devices from ever communicating with each other
questions.explain: Segmentation — placing servers, workstations, and guest/IoT devices in separate subnets — lets different access controls and monitoring apply to each group, a core defense-in-depth principle.
